conceptTag: Design a model for a coffee brand
readerTitle: Design a business model for a new coffee brand
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (대형 식품회사 안의 신규 사업팀이 사무실용 커피 브랜드를 설계) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업 모델은 누가 내는가, 무엇에 돈을 받는가, 어떻게 공급하는가, 얼마가 남는가라는 네 가지 답이 서로 맞물린 묶음이다.
misconception: 제품이 좋으면 돈 버는 방법은 나중에 저절로 정해진다.

sources.text: 모든 수치와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시
BMO-01 유닛의 표준 개념 (사용자와 지불자, 수익원, 비용 구조, 자산 경량·중량, 마진)

factChecks.note: 사무실 한 곳 월 계산: 요금 $400 − 원두 $150 − 머신 리스 $70 − 서비스 $40 = $140, 140 ÷ 400 = 35%. 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
선택지 피드백의 결과(사용량 감소, 가입 수 등)는 가상 시나리오 안의 결과이며 실제 연구나 기업 데이터가 아닙니다. 모든 시나리오 카드에 illustrative 라벨을 붙였습니다.

cards.title: You have one year to turn good coffee into a business.
body: You lead a five-person team inside a large food company. Leadership wants its own coffee brand. You get one year and a modest budget to prove the model.
The coffee is good. That part is done. Over the next four decisions, you design how it makes money.

image.label: A small team around a table with coffee bags and a whiteboard
image.brief: 대기업 사무실 한쪽 회의실. 다섯 명의 팀이 원두 봉투와 화이트보드 앞에 모여 있음. 화이트보드에 "Who pays? / What do we charge for? / How do we supply it? / What's left?" 네 줄. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Office workers love it. Who should pay?
body: Your free trial in 10 offices went well. Staff drink several cups a day and ask for more. Supermarket shelves, your other option, are crowded and expensive to get onto.

options.text: Each employee, per cup, through a payment app
options.feedback: You charge the people who enjoy it, but every cup now comes with a small payment decision. In your trial offices, drinking drops and the habit fades.

options.text: The employer, as a monthly fee per office
options.feedback: Employers already pay for perks that keep staff happy. You get one buyer and one invoice, and the drinkers never think about price.

options.text: Nobody yet. Keep it free to build the brand for supermarkets
options.feedback: Free builds fans, but it captures none of the value you create. The costly supermarket fight is still ahead of you.

cards.title: Say you chose the employer. What do you charge for?
body: Each office needs a machine, beans, and someone to fix things when they break. Which pricing fits?

options.text: Sell the machine upfront, then sell beans by the bag
options.feedback: Simple to explain, but the big upfront price scares small offices. Bean orders can also drift to a cheaper supplier.

options.text: One monthly fee for machine, service and a set amount of beans; extra beans billed per kilo
options.feedback: Revenue repeats every month and grows with use. Heavy drinkers pay more instead of eating your profit.

options.text: One flat monthly fee, unlimited coffee
options.feedback: Easy to sell. But your thirstiest offices cost the most, and they are the ones most eager to sign up.

cards.softwareNote: Software pricing faces the same choice. A base subscription plus usage on top keeps heavy users from turning into losses, which an unlimited plan can't do.

cards.title: Say you chose the monthly fee. Demand is growing.
body: Fifty offices sign up in six months. Leadership hopes for hundreds, but nobody knows yet. How do you get machines and service?

image.label: Coffee machines lined up in a warehouse, some still in boxes
image.brief: 창고 안에 사무실용 커피 머신이 줄지어 있고 절반은 아직 상자에 들어 있음. 한쪽엔 작업복 차림 기술자. 불확실한 수요를 암시하도록 빈 선반도 보이게. 실제 제조사 로고 없음.

options.text: Buy 500 machines and hire your own technicians
options.feedback: Cheapest per machine if demand arrives. If it doesn't, you carry idle machines and salaries every month.

options.text: Lease machines and pay a service partner per visit
options.feedback: Each office costs a bit more, but costs rise only as offices sign up. You can buy later, once demand is proven.

options.text: Ask the parent company to build a roastery for the brand
options.feedback: Owning roasting could cut bean costs later. Today it adds a large fixed cost before the model has proven itself.

cards.title: Say you chose to lease. Here's one office, one month.
body: That **$140** pays for your team's salaries and marketing first. Only what's left after that is profit.

cards.title: A big client wants 30% off.
body: A bank wants your coffee in 40 branch offices if you cut the fee by 30%, from $400 to $280. Your sales lead is thrilled.

options.text: Accept. Forty offices is a huge win
options.feedback: Each office would leave $20 instead of $140. Forty offices add just $800 a month, and one price rise from your bean supplier wipes it out.

options.text: Counter with 10% off in exchange for a two-year contract
options.feedback: At $360, each office leaves $100, or $4,000 a month across 40. The commitment also makes buying your own machines safer later.
Your margin stays intact, but you lose a client that could speed your growth. Some discount can be worth it for volume and commitment.

cards.title: The best answers depend on the setup.
body: This story assumed uncertain demand and a tight deadline. With five-year contracts in hand, owning machines might be smarter. Where staff already buy their own coffee, charging per cup could work.
Teams inside big companies face one more trap. The parent's spare factory, trucks or sales staff can look free. They aren't. **Count them as costs**, or your model will look better than it really is.

image.label: A scale weighing 'borrowed from parent company' against 'real costs'
image.brief: 저울 그림. 한쪽 접시에 "Borrowed from parent: trucks, warehouse, sales team" 아이콘, 다른 쪽에 "Real costs" 라벨의 동전 더미. 공짜처럼 보이는 자원도 무게가 있다는 느낌으로 저울이 균형을 이루게.

cards.title: A business model is four answers that fit together.
body: Each decision you made is one idea from this unit:
list: **Who pays:** the employer, not the drinker *(who uses vs who pays)*
**What you charge for:** a monthly fee plus usage *(revenue streams)*
**How you supply it:** lease until demand is proven *(cost structure, asset-light vs asset-heavy)*
**What's left:** $140 per office, so 30% off nearly erases it *(margins)*
cards.callout: **Try it today:** answer these four questions for your own business in one line each. Circle the answer you're least sure of.
